source.title: On the Convergence of SARAH and Beyond
source.authors: Bing-Cong Li; Meng Ma; G. Giannakis

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper; no relevant section is visibly cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a neural-network experiment comparing L2S with other optimizers on held-out accuracy and training loss, bearing on generalization across training methods. It does not test any listed version's specific claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's logistic-regression convergence results and cited claims about sharp minima are not rows. Figure 2 values are not numerically recoverable from the text; the Results description gives qualitative comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study compares variance-reduction optimizers on MNIST, but none is an adaptive optimizer of the kind named in V4. It does not vary batch size or measure sharpness, so its discussion of large batches and sharp minima does not test V5 or V7. Its own results test none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the authors' qualified claim that L2S can generalize better than SARAH, supported by their MNIST experiment. Their explanation that the accuracy drop reflects movement between local minima is an interpretation, not a measured mechanism. The paper's overall conclusion emphasizes its unified optimization framework and convergence guarantees.
record.recipe_differences: The experiment compares the LoopLess SARAH algorithm with SARAH, SVRG and SGD; it does not test random-label memorization or the listed interventions and measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relative test-accuracy performance changes over effective passes: L2S is initially comparable to SARAH, then begins to outperform it around 140 effective passes.

fits_no_version.finding: For a 784 × 128 × 10 sigmoid network on MNIST, L2S and SARAH perform comparably earlier in training; around 140 effective passes, L2S begins to outperform SARAH following a deep accuracy drop. L2S also fluctuates more.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Randomizing snapshot-gradient scheduling can improve late-training held-out accuracy relative to SARAH in this MNIST experiment.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The neural-network comparison is limited to one MNIST feedforward network and the plotted outcomes; exact numerical values and uncertainty estimates are not provided in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant result rows were identified. The paper's other numerical tests concern logistic-regression optimization convergence, not the claim's generalization outcomes.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance under random versus natural labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning, weight-decay, or switching recipes.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce the penalty; all neural-network experiments use batch size 32.
Dropout, weight decay, training-set size, and augmentation interventions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The cited large-batch finding and schematic illustration of sharp versus flat minima are background, not independent results. No verdict labels apply.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization, natural-label generalization after fitting random labels, and the named architectures and datasets.
Width sweeps, interpolation threshold, and test error as width increases.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under limited or broader tuning; the comparison here is L2S versus SARAH and other variance-reduction methods.
Batch-size comparisons and fixed-epoch large-batch effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removal of memorized examples and its effect on test accuracy.
